titulo.texto: Stirrup-Handle Vessel from the Capacha Complex

frase_gancho.texto: A vessel more than three thousand years old that poses a mystery of the sea.

puente_narrativo.texto: From the oldest villages, we move on to an archaeological rescue. Look for a female figure of painted clay, with wide hips and a body covered in geometric designs.

guion_corto.texto: This gray vessel, about twenty-five centimeters tall, comes from Colima and is among the oldest in the West: it was made about three thousand five hundred years ago. It is formed by two rounded bodies, one on top of the other, joined by curved tubes that look like handles; this type of handle is called a stirrup handle. The surface is polished and decorated with incised lines, made with an awl while the clay was still damp. Notice the shape, which recalls a double gourd. It was made by hand, without a wheel. At that time the people of Colima lived in villages, grew maize, and buried their dead in simple pits, with vessels like this one. It is not a luxury object, but one of the first signs of the pottery talent of the West.

guion_largo.texto:
This vessel resembles others found thousands of kilometers from here, and no one knows for certain why. That makes it one of the most interesting pieces in the hall: a question made of clay.

It is called Capacha after a place in Colima where the archaeologist Isabel Kelly found the first cemeteries with vessels of this type. Her discovery showed that in Colima there were villages as ancient as those of Tlatilco, which you saw in the hall of the first villages, or as those of the first Olmec. In other words, while colossal heads were being raised at San Lorenzo, in Colima an elegant, carefully made pottery was already being produced.

Now, the mystery. Vessels with a double body and a stirrup handle almost identical to this one appear in Ecuador, in the cultures known as Machalilla and Chorrera, more than three thousand kilometers away, following the Pacific coast. Coincidence? Some think so: simple forms that were invented separately in different places. Others maintain that there was contact by sea from very ancient times, with navigators who traveled along the coast. There is no consensus, and that is why the piece is so famous among specialists.

This debate is not a whim. Further on, in this same hall, you will see another clue of the same kind: metallurgy, the technique of working metal that you saw in the [gold pectoral from Tomb 7](mna_s07_pectoral_oro_tumba7) at Monte Albán. According to many specialists, it reached the West from South America around the year seven hundred of our era. If there were voyages by sea, this vessel would be one of the first signs.

Think about how the person who used it lived. These were small villages, near the coast and the valleys, where maize, beans, and squash were grown, and food was supplemented with hunting and fishing. There were no cities or pyramids. Even so, these villagers devoted time to shaping a two-bodied vessel by hand, polishing it with a smooth stone, and decorating it with a bone awl. Beauty did not wait for kings to exist.

When an archaeologist speaks of a pottery “complex,” such as the Capacha complex, they mean a set of forms and decorations that appear together in the same time and place. It is the way to recognize a culture when we have neither its name nor its writing: by the trace of its hands in the clay.

Notice, too, the shape. It imitates a gourd, the dry fruit that has been used as a container for millennia: two spheres joined by a neck. In many communities in Mexico, the gourd is still used today to carry water. The potters of Capacha took a form from nature and turned it into clay.

Vessels like this one appear in tombs, beside the body. It is thought that they held water or drinks for the dead person’s journey. And the tombs were simple: pits with stone slabs on top, without pyramids or chambers. The tradition of deep tombs, which you will see next, would arrive almost one thousand five hundred years later. But care for the dead is already here.

Thus begins the West hall: with a humble vessel, polished by hand, that still asks questions.

texto.Period: Early Preclassic, Formative (1500-1000 BC; around 1450 BC)
texto.Material: Polished dark brown or black clay ceramic, with fine incisions and stippled fields
texto.Origin: Colima (type site at the old Capacha hacienda), with spread toward Jalisco and Michoacán

texto.pregunta: Myth: The ancient cultures of Mexico lived isolated from one another.
texto.respuesta: Reality: There was exchange over great distances, by land and perhaps by sea. Some vessels from Colima resemble others from Ecuador, and it is debated whether there was maritime contact.
